intro: Five tasks bring the module together: photons and the energy levels of an atom, radioactive decay and its energy, measuring radiation and radiation safety, elementary particles and the early universe, and fission and nuclear power. In each one you decide which models fit the situation and justify your choice.

tasks.title: Aurora
tasks.source_note: Energy levels and spectral lines of the oxygen atom: NIST Atomic Spectra Database (checked 2026), rounded. The lifetimes of the excited states and the altitudes of auroras are typical values from the literature.
tasks.text:
Electrons of the solar wind plunge into the upper atmosphere in the polar regions and collide with oxygen atoms. A collision can excite an oxygen atom, and when the excited state decays, the light of the aurora is produced. The most common colours of the aurora are green, $557.7\,\text{nm}$, and red, $630.0\,\text{nm}$, and both are produced in transitions between the three lowest energy levels of the oxygen atom. The figure shows these energy levels.

Planck's constant is $h = 6.626 \cdot 10^{-34}\,\text{J}\,\text{s}$, the speed of light $c = 2.998 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{m/s}$ and $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$.

parts.text: Which transitions produce the green and the red light? Justify by calculating. One more transition is possible between these three levels. Calculate the wavelength of the radiation it produces. Can it be seen in the aurora?

criteria.text: Calculates the photon energy of each colour, $2.22\,\text{eV}$ and $1.97\,\text{eV}$, and connects it to the difference of the levels in the figure: green from the second excited state to the lower one, red from the first excited state to the ground state.

criteria.detail: The photon energy is the difference of the levels, $E = \dfrac{hc}{\lambda}$, so $\lambda = \dfrac{hc}{E}$; the third transition is from the second excited state directly to the ground state, $E = 4.19\,\text{eV}$.
$\lambda \approx 296\,\text{nm}$, when the electronvolts have been converted to joules by substitution.
The wavelength is in the ultraviolet region, shorter than the lower limit of visible light, about $380\,\text{nm}$, so the eye cannot see it.

parts.text: The kinetic energy of an electron that produces an aurora is typically about $5\,\text{keV}$. At most how many oxygen atoms can one such electron excite to the second excited state? What did you assume?

criteria.text: Justifies that in every exciting collision the electron loses at least the difference of the levels, $4.19\,\text{eV}$, so the number of excitations is at most the quotient of the kinetic energy and this energy.

criteria.detail: $5000\,\text{eV} : 4.19\,\text{eV} \approx 1190$, when $1\,\text{keV} = 1000\,\text{eV}$ has been substituted.
Assumption: all the energy is used for this excitation. In reality part of it goes to ionisation, to exciting nitrogen molecules and to other levels, so there are fewer excitations.

parts.text: Red aurora is produced mostly at altitudes above $200\,\text{km}$, green at about $100$–$150\,\text{km}$, where the air is much denser. The second excited state decays on average about $0.7\,\text{s}$ after the excitation, the lower one only after about $110\,\text{s}$. Using this information, explain why red light is not produced lower down. Also explain why the spectrum of the light of the aurora consists of separate lines.

criteria.text: Explains that the energy of an atom can have only certain values, so the energy of a photon, and therefore the wavelength, always corresponds to the difference of some two levels, and the spectrum has only these lines.

Explains that in dense air an excited atom collides with another particle much more often than once in $110\,\text{s}$, and the collision releases the excited state so that the energy goes to the other particle and no photon is produced.
Explains that the lifetime of the upper level, $0.7\,\text{s}$, is so short that many atoms have time to emit a green photon before a collision even in denser air.

criteria.detail: Red light requires thin air, where there are few collisions: this is why it is produced high up, and the explanation is tied to the given altitudes and lifetimes.

parts.text: The sensor of a camera that photographs auroras is silicon. A pixel detects a photon if the energy of the photon is enough to raise an electron from the valence band of silicon to the conduction band. At least $1.12\,\text{eV}$ is needed for this. What is the longest wavelength that the sensor can detect? A camera salesperson claims: "When the infrared radiation is intense enough, the sensor also detects radiation of $1500\,\text{nm}$." Evaluate the claim.

criteria.detail: The longest wavelength corresponds to the smallest sufficient photon energy: $\lambda_\text{max} = \dfrac{hc}{E}$.
$\lambda_\text{max} \approx 1110\,\text{nm}$ (about $1.1\,\mu\text{m}$); so the sensor detects the green and red light of the aurora.

criteria.text: Calculates or justifies that the energy of a $1500\,\text{nm}$ photon, about $0.83\,\text{eV}$, is smaller than $1.12\,\text{eV}$.
Explains that more intense radiation means more photons, not a greater photon energy: no single photon raises an electron to the conduction band, so the claim is false.

tasks.title: Power source of a Mars rover
tasks.source_note: NASA, data on the MMRTG generator (Curiosity and Perseverance), rounded; atomic masses AME2020; half-lives NNDC (checked 2026).
tasks.text:
The Mars rovers Curiosity and Perseverance get their electricity from a radioisotope generator. The generator contains $4.8\,\text{kg}$ of plutonium dioxide $\text{PuO}_2$, most of whose plutonium is plutonium-238. Plutonium-238 decays by alpha decay into uranium-234. The energy of the decay is turned into heat in the generator, and thermocouples turn part of the heat into electricity. At launch the thermal power of the generator was about $2000\,\text{W}$ and the electrical power about $110\,\text{W}$.

| substance | atomic mass $(\text{u})$ |
|---|---|
| ${}^{238}_{94}\text{Pu}$ | $238.049560$ |
| ${}^{234}_{92}\text{U}$ | $234.040952$ |
| ${}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$ | $4.002603$ |

The half-life of plutonium-238 is $87.7\,\text{a}$. In addition, $1\,\text{u} = 931.5\,\tfrac{\text{MeV}}{c^2} = 1.66054 \cdot 10^{-27}\,\text{kg}$, $1\,\text{eV} = 1.602 \cdot 10^{-19}\,\text{J}$ and $1\,\text{a} = 365.25\,\text{d}$.

Other radioactive substances could also be considered as fuel for the generator:

| substance | decay | half-life |
|---|---|---|
| polonium-210 | $\alpha$ | $138\,\text{d}$ |
| cobalt-60 | $\beta^-$, strong $\gamma$ | $5.27\,\text{a}$ |
| plutonium-238 | $\alpha$ | $87.7\,\text{a}$ |
| uranium-238 | $\alpha$ | $4.47 \cdot 10^{9}\,\text{a}$ |

parts.text: Write the reaction equation of the decay. How much energy does one decay release?

criteria.text: Reaction equation ${}^{238}_{94}\text{Pu} \rightarrow {}^{234}_{92}\text{U} + {}^{4}_{2}\text{He}$, in which the nucleon number and the charge are conserved.

criteria.detail: $Q = (m_\text{Pu} - m_\text{U} - m_\text{He})\,c^2$ with atomic masses; the number of electrons is the same on both sides, so their masses cancel.
The mass defect is $0.006005\,\text{u}$, and $1\,\text{u} = 931.5\,\tfrac{\text{MeV}}{c^2}$ has been substituted.
$Q \approx 5.59\,\text{MeV}$

parts.text: How many kilograms of plutonium-238 must the generator contain for its thermal power to be $2000\,\text{W}$? What fraction of the plutonium of the generator is then plutonium-238? Assume that the whole energy of the decay is turned into heat in the generator.

criteria.text: Justifies that the activity is the power divided by the energy of one decay, $A = \dfrac{P}{Q} \approx 2.2 \cdot 10^{15}\,\text{Bq}$, when $Q$ has been converted to joules.

criteria.detail: $A = \lambda N$, where $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln 2}{T_{1/2}}$ and $T_{1/2}$ is in seconds, and $m = N m_\text{Pu}$.
$m \approx 3.5\,\text{kg}$
The plutonium makes up $238 : 270$ of the $\text{PuO}_2$, so there is about $4.2\,\text{kg}$ of plutonium, and about $83\,\%$ of it is plutonium-238 and the rest are other isotopes of plutonium.

parts.text: Why is plutonium-238 chosen for a flight lasting decades? For each of the other substances in the table, justify why it is rejected. What is important for radiation safety when the generator is assembled and launched from Earth?

criteria.text: Polonium-210: the half-life is short compared with the flight; the power would fall to about one sixth already in a year.
Uranium-238: the activity per nucleus is inversely proportional to the half-life, so it is about $5 \cdot 10^{7}$ times smaller than for plutonium-238, and the required mass would be enormous.
Cobalt-60: the penetrating gamma radiation would require heavy shielding and would damage the electronics, whereas alpha particles stop already in the fuel and their energy is turned into heat.

Explains that alpha radiation does not penetrate the shell of the generator, but plutonium is very dangerous inside the body: this is why the fuel is a durable ceramic in capsules that must not break in a launch accident.

parts.text: How large is the thermal power of the generator $14$ years after the launch? How large would the electrical power be if the efficiency of the generator stayed the same? According to NASA, the real electrical power has decreased faster. What can be the reason for this?

criteria.text: Justifies that the thermal power is proportional to the activity and thus to the number of undecayed nuclei, so it decreases according to the decay law: $P = P_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}$.

criteria.detail: $P \approx 1790\,\text{W}$
The electrical power with the same efficiency is $110\,\text{W} \cdot 0.895 \approx 98\,\text{W}$.
The calculation assumed the efficiency to be constant. The thermocouples age, so the efficiency decreases, and the decay law gives only an upper limit for the electrical power.

parts.text: The alpha radiation of plutonium-238 is especially harmful if the substance gets into the body. Suppose that in a launch accident plutonium dioxide dust with an activity of $10\,\text{Bq}$ remained in a person's lungs and that the dust stayed in the lungs for a whole year. The mass of the lungs is $1.2\,\text{kg}$, the radiation weighting factor of alpha radiation is $20$ and the tissue weighting factor of lung tissue is $0.12$. How large an effective dose would this cause in a year? Compare the result with the average annual dose of a person in Finland, $5.9\,\text{mSv}$.

criteria.text: Justifies that alpha particles stop in the lung tissue, so in a year it absorbs the energy $E = AtQ$, when the activity stays approximately constant for the year, and calculates $E \approx 2.8 \cdot 10^{-4}\,\text{J}$.

criteria.detail: $D = \dfrac{E}{m}$, $H_\text{T} = w_\text{R} D$ and $H_\text{E} = w_\text{T} H_\text{T}$.
$H_\text{E} \approx 0.57\,\text{mSv}$, that is, about $0.6\,\text{mSv}$ a year.

The dose is about a tenth of the average annual dose in Finland, even though $10\,\text{Bq}$ is a very small activity: inside the body an alpha emitter is dangerous, and this is why plutonium is prevented from entering the body.

tasks.title: The school's caesium source
tasks.source_note: The pulse counts have been calculated from a model, and random variation has been added to them as in a measurement; they are not the results of a real measurement. Dose rate of background radiation outdoors: STUK (2026).
tasks.text:
In an upper secondary school physics classroom there is a sealed caesium-137 radiation source. Under the supervision of the teacher, the students placed the source with tongs in front of a GM tube and counted the pulses for $1.0\,\text{min}$ at different distances $r$. The distance was measured from the source to the window of the tube with a millimetre scale. Before the measurement they measured the background radiation without the source and got $112$ pulses in $5.0\,\text{min}$.

| $r\ (\text{cm})$ | pulses in $1.0\,\text{min}$ |
|---|---|
| $2.0$ | $3048$ |
| $3.0$ | $1806$ |
| $4.0$ | $1172$ |
| $5.0$ | $790$ |
| $6.0$ | $617$ |
| $8.0$ | $405$ |
| $10.0$ | $256$ |
| $14.0$ | $152$ |
| $20.0$ | $94$ |

Radioactive decay is random. When $N$ pulses are counted, the random variation in their number is about $\sqrt{N}$.

parts.text: A student assumes that the source is a point source, its radiation spreads evenly in all directions and the tube always detects the same fraction of the photons that hit its window. Draw a graph whose points should lie on a straight line through the origin according to this assumption. What can be concluded from the graph?

criteria.text: Subtracts the background $22.4\,\tfrac{1}{\text{min}}$ from every reading and justifies that the radiation is spread over the surface of a sphere $4\pi r^2$, so according to the model the net count rate $R$ is proportional to $\tfrac{1}{r^2}$.

criteria.detail: $\tfrac{1}{r^2}$ on the horizontal axis in the unit $\tfrac{1}{\text{cm}^2}$ and $R$ on the vertical axis in the unit $\tfrac{1}{\text{min}}$.
There is no straight line through the origin that fits all the points: the nearest points fall below the line drawn through the distant points.

The assumption does not hold as such near the source: the count rate increases more slowly than $\tfrac{1}{r^2}$ as the source is approached. The most probable reason is that the measured distance $r$ is not the distance to the detection point of the tube.

parts.text: The teacher points out that the sensitive volume of a GM tube is behind the window. The model can be valid if the distance is taken to be $r + d$, where $d$ is the distance between the window and the effective detection point of the tube. Draw from the data a graph whose points should lie on a straight line according to this model, and determine $d$ from it.

criteria.text: Justifies that from the model $R = \dfrac{K}{(r + d)^2}$ we get $\dfrac{1}{\sqrt{R}} = \dfrac{r + d}{\sqrt{K}}$, so $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{R}}$ is a first-degree function of $r$, and the line crosses the $r$ axis at $r = -d$.

criteria.detail: The points $(r;\ \tfrac{1}{\sqrt{R}})$ calculated from the net count rates.
A line that fits all the points, extended as far as the $r$ axis.
The intercept on the $r$ axis read or calculated from two distant points of the line.
$d \approx 1.3\,\text{cm}$; $1.0$–$1.6\,\text{cm}$ is accepted.

parts.text: Estimate the uncertainty of the net count rates at $2.0\,\text{cm}$ and $20\,\text{cm}$. Which measuring point is more uncertain and why? How could the measurement be improved?

criteria.detail: $20\,\text{cm}$: $\Delta N \approx \sqrt{94} \approx 10$, so the net count rate $72 \pm 10\,\tfrac{1}{\text{min}}$ is uncertain by about $14\,\%$; $2.0\,\text{cm}$: $\sqrt{3048} \approx 55$, that is, only about $2\,\%$.
Near the source the error in reading the distance is emphasised: an error of $1\,\text{mm}$ changes the count rate by about $6\,\%$, because $R$ depends on the square of the distance.

criteria.text: Suggests a longer counting time for the distant points (the relative random variation decreases like $\tfrac{1}{\sqrt{N}}$) and more precise setting of the distance for the near points, for example with a stand.

parts.text: A student concludes: "When the net count rate of the source has decreased to the size of the background, no radiation comes from the source any more, and farther away there is no need to think about radiation safety." At what distance $r$ is the net count rate, according to the model of part b, equal to the count rate of the background? According to the manufacturer of the source, the dose rate at $10\,\text{cm}$ from the source is about $3.0\,\mu\text{Sv/h}$, and outdoors in Finland the dose rate of background radiation is usually $0.05$–$0.30\,\mu\text{Sv/h}$. Evaluate the student's reasoning.

criteria.detail: $\dfrac{K}{(r + d)^2} = R_\text{t}$, so $r = \sqrt{\dfrac{K}{R_\text{t}}} - d$, and $K = \dfrac{1}{k^2}$ from the slope $k$ of the line of part b.
$r \approx 36\,\text{cm}$
The dose rate at this distance is about $3.0\,\mu\text{Sv/h} \cdot \left(\tfrac{10\,\text{cm}}{36\,\text{cm}}\right)^2 \approx 0.2\,\mu\text{Sv/h}$.

The radiation does not stop; its dose rate decreases to the order of magnitude of the background, and the tube can no longer distinguish it from the variation of the background. The reasoning is wrong, but distance is a good means of protection.

tasks.title: The first minutes
tasks.source_note: Particle Data Group, Review of Particle Physics 2024: masses of particles, mean lifetime of the neutron $878.4\,\text{s}$ (half-life $609\,\text{s}$) and the observed mass fraction of helium $0.245$, rounded.
tasks.text:
Observations of the oldest stars and gas clouds tell us that after the first minutes of the universe about $24.5\,\%$ of the mass of ordinary matter was helium-4 and the rest almost entirely hydrogen. About $1\,\text{s}$ after the Big Bang there were about $6$ protons for every neutron. After that the ratio of the numbers of neutrons and protons changed only as free neutrons decayed. Nuclei could not yet form, because the photons of the hot radiation broke up the deuterium nuclei that were formed. When nuclei finally formed, almost all of the remaining neutrons ended up in helium-4 nuclei.

| particle | mass $(\tfrac{\text{MeV}}{c^2})$ |
|---|---|
| neutron $n$ | $939.565$ |
| proton $p$ | $938.272$ |
| electron $e^-$ | $0.511$ |

The half-life of a free neutron is $609\,\text{s}$.

parts.text: A free neutron decays, but a free proton does not decay into a neutron. Explain why, using the masses of the particles. What happens to the quarks in the decay, and which interaction causes it?

criteria.text: Calculates that the mass of the neutron is $0.782\,\tfrac{\text{MeV}}{c^2}$ greater than that of the proton and the electron together, so the decay releases energy; the change of a proton into a neutron would require energy.
Decay equation $n \rightarrow p + e^- + \bar{\nu}_e$, in which the charge is conserved.
One $d$ quark of the neutron ($udd$) changes into a $u$ quark, which produces a proton ($uud$).
The change is caused by the weak interaction, whose mediator particle is the $W^-$ boson.

parts.text: How many protons were there for every neutron when nuclei formed? What did you assume?

criteria.text: Justifies that every helium-4 nucleus contains two neutrons and two protons, so the mass of the helium is approximately $2N_n$ nucleon masses, when the mass of all nucleons is $N_n + N_p$ nucleon masses.

criteria.detail: About $7.2$ protons per neutron.
The masses of the proton and the neutron are assumed equal and the binding energy small; the neutrons left in deuterium and lithium are ignored.

parts.text: How long after the Big Bang did nuclei begin to form?

criteria.text: Justifies that every decayed neutron becomes a proton, so there are always $7$ nucleons for every original neutron, and solves that $0.858$ neutrons are then left.

criteria.detail: $N = N_0 \left(\tfrac{1}{2}\right)^{t / T_{1/2}}$ solved for time, for example using a logarithm.
$t \approx 0.222 \cdot 609\,\text{s} \approx 135\,\text{s}$ from the moment $1\,\text{s}$.
About $140\,\text{s}$, that is, about $2\,\text{min}$ after the Big Bang.

parts.text: The ratio of neutrons to protons at the moment $1\,\text{s}$ is known only approximately. A student claims: "If the ratio had been $1 : 5$ and not $1 : 6$, the result of part c would change only a little, so the method is reliable." Evaluate the claim by calculating. What else does the result of part c require? According to more accurate models, nuclei began to form about three minutes after the Big Bang. How well does the result of part c agree with this?

criteria.detail: With the ratio $1 : 5$ there are $0.735$ neutrons left, and the time is about $270\,\text{s}$, that is, about $4.5\,\text{min}$.
The claim is false: the time almost doubles, because only a small fraction of the neutrons has time to decay, and then a small change in the initial ratio changes the time a lot.
Part c assumes that after the moment $1\,\text{s}$ neutrons changed into protons only in the decay of free neutrons and that the nuclei formed at a single moment.

criteria.text: Compares the result of part c with the about three minutes of the more accurate models and states that the order of magnitude is right: minutes, not seconds or hours.

tasks.title: Natural reactor at Oklo
tasks.source_note: Proportions of isotopes IUPAC, half-lives NNDC (checked 2026); data on Oklo: Gauthier-Lafaye et al. (1996) and Meshik (2005), rounded order-of-magnitude estimate.
tasks.text:
In 1972 French researchers noticed that in the uranium ore of the Oklo mine in Gabon the proportion of uranium-235 in the uranium was in places only $0.440\,\%$. Everywhere else on Earth it is $0.720\,\%$, and the remaining $99.274\,\%$ is uranium-238. The researchers concluded that about $2.0$ billion years ago a natural fission reactor had operated in the ore, in which groundwater that had seeped into the ore acted as the moderator. The reactor worked in cycles: about half an hour running and then a pause of a couple of hours.

| nucleus | half-life |
|---|---|
| uranium-235 | $7.04 \cdot 10^{8}\,\text{a}$ |
| uranium-238 | $4.47 \cdot 10^{9}\,\text{a}$ |
| plutonium-239 | $24\,100\,\text{a}$ |

In the fuel of present-day light-water reactors the proportion of uranium-235 is $3$–$5\,\%$; with natural uranium a chain reaction cannot be sustained with light water.

parts.text: What percentage of the uranium was uranium-235 $2.0$ billion years ago? Why was a chain reaction then possible but not now?

criteria.text: Justifies that each isotope decays with its own half-life, and calculates the number of nuclei of each backwards in time, for example $0.720$ and $99.274$ per present-day nucleus.

criteria.detail: $N_0 = N \cdot 2^{t / T_{1/2}}$ for each isotope, and the proportion $\dfrac{N_{235}}{N_{235} + N_{238}}$.
The factors $2^{2.841} \approx 7.17$ and $2^{0.447} \approx 1.36$.
The proportion was then the same as in the enriched fuel of present-day reactors, so water was enough as a moderator; now the $0.72\,\%$ of natural uranium is too little.

parts.text: What does the unusually small proportion of uranium-235 tell us? Explain how groundwater made the reactor both start and stop in cycles.

criteria.text: Explains that uranium-235 is exactly what is used up in fission, because it undergoes fission easily when a slow neutron hits it; this is why its proportion decreased in the ore.
Explains that water slowed down the fast neutrons produced in fission, so that they caused new fissions and the multiplication factor rose to one.
Explains that the heat of the fissions boiled the water away; without a moderator the multiplication factor fell below one, and the chain reaction stopped.
Explains that the ore cooled, the water returned and the reaction started again, which fits the observed cycles.

parts.text: According to estimates, the combined thermal power of the Oklo reactors was on average about $100\,\text{kW}$, and they operated in cycles for a total of about $150\,000$ years. How long does it take the reactor of Olkiluoto 3, whose thermal power is $4300\,\text{MW}$, to produce the same energy?

criteria.detail: Energy is power times time, $P_\text{O} t_\text{O} = P_\text{OL3} t_\text{OL3}$, so $t_\text{OL3} = \dfrac{P_\text{O}}{P_\text{OL3}}\, t_\text{O}$.
About $3.5\,\text{a}$, when the powers have been converted to the same unit.
The power of the natural reactor was about $43\,000$ times smaller than that of Olkiluoto 3, but it operated about $43\,000$ times longer: it was small but very long-lived.

parts.text: An author claims: "The fission products and plutonium at Oklo have stayed in place in the bedrock for two billion years. Therefore it is certain that spent fuel disposed of in Onkalo will stay safely in place." Plutonium-239 decays by alpha decay into uranium-235. How can it be concluded from Oklo at all whether the plutonium stayed in place? Evaluate the claim.

criteria.text: States that there is no plutonium-239 left, because in two billion years about $83\,000$ half-lives have passed, and concludes that its staying in place is seen from its decay product, uranium-235.

criteria.detail: The claim assumes that the conditions in Onkalo are similar to those at Oklo. The bedrock, the chemistry of the groundwater and the form of the waste are different, so an observation at one place does not transfer as such.
Oklo is a strong example of how bedrock can retain many substances for a long time, but "certain" is too strong a word: one natural example does not prove the safety of another place.

criteria.text: Tells what the safety of Onkalo is based on: a copper canister, bentonite clay and deep bedrock, whose operation is studied with experiments and models for hundreds of thousands of years.
